definition.text: China's national emissions trading system for carbon dioxide, which caps emissions per unit of output rather than in total, and began operating in 2021.

facts.text: China proposed a carbon tax in 2010 but never passed it, setting up an emissions trading scheme in February 2021 instead.
It began with power plants and covers 40% of China's emissions, which is 15% of world emissions; it is the largest scheme of its kind.
In July 2021 permits were handed out free and traded at around RMB 50 per tonne, roughly half the EU ETS price.
Seven pilot markets, starting in Shenzhen on June 18, 2013, preceded it, with compliance rates over 96%.
Studies find it cut carbon emissions by up to 18.2%, cut power sector emissions by 13% in 2013-2020, and delivered about a third of China's air pollution health benefits.
Some researchers found it can reduce GDP or hold back innovation.
By 2027 it is expected to cover all major industrial emitters and move to an absolute cap on emissions for stable sectors.

definition.text: A Kyoto Protocol credit for one tonne of CO2 equivalent cut by a Joint Implementation project.

facts.text: Landfill gas capture is an example: methane has a 100-year global warming potential of 25 compared with carbon dioxide.
Burning one tonne of captured methane yields nearly 3 tonnes of CO2, a saving of 22 ERUs.
ERU prices declined 89 percent in 2012, falling to 15 euro cents in December.

title: European Union Emissions Trading System

definition.text: The European Union's cap-and-trade scheme for greenhouse gases, begun in 2005, in which each allowance permits its holder to emit 1 ton of CO2.

facts.text: It was the first large greenhouse gas trading scheme in the world and operates in 30 countries: the 27 EU states plus Iceland, Liechtenstein and Norway.
As of 2026 it covers around 40% of the EU's emissions; its cap should reach zero by 2039.
Between 2005 and 2023, emissions from covered power plants and factories fell by 47%.
A 2023 study found it cut emissions by 10% between 2005 and 2012 with no significant effect on profits or employment.
Phase I over-allocation drove the carbon price to zero in 2007.
It has been criticised for over-allocation, windfall profits, price volatility and failure to meet its goals.
Auction revenue in 2013 - 2025 exceeded €245 billion, most of it going directly to member states.
It has suffered fraud: hackers stole 28 to 30 million euros of allowances in 2011, and VAT fraud cost Germany about €850 million.

contested_note: Critics say it has failed its goals through over-allocation and windfall profits, while proponents call Phase I a learning phase and point to measured cuts.

title: Market Stability Reserve
article: European Union Emissions Trading System#Reform of the EU-ETS and introduction of the Market Stability Reserve (MSR)

definition.text: An EU ETS mechanism that changes how many permits are auctioned each year according to how many surplus permits are in circulation.

facts.text: It runs on predefined rules with no discretion for the Commission or member states.
Back-loading and the MSR law failed to cut the surplus or lift prices in 2014–2017, when prices stayed below €10/tCO2.
Since 2023, allowances in the reserve above a threshold are permanently invalidated; about 2.5 billion were invalidated on 1 January 2023.

definition.text: A second EU emissions trading system for carbon dioxide from buildings, road transport and other sectors outside the original ETS.

facts.text: It covers emissions upstream: fuel suppliers, not end consumers, must report and pay for them.
Its cap aims for a 42% cut by 2030 compared with 2005, with revenue partly funding a Social Climate Fund for vulnerable groups.
Together the two systems will cover 75% of EU greenhouse gas emissions.
In 2025 its start was delayed to 2028 under pressure from member states worried about inflation and energy affordability.
